background.definition: Melanoma is a malignant tumor that originates in melanocytes, the cells that produce the pigment melanin that colors our skin, hair, and eyes. It may begin in a mole (skin melanoma), but can also begin in other pigmented tissues, such as in the eye or in the intestines.

list.listitem: An estimated 62,480 people will develop melanoma of the skin in 2008 in the United States. An additional 54,020 cases of melanoma in situ are expected to be newly diagnosed in the United States in 2008.

In a 5-year period in the United States, the incidence of melanoma increased 2.4-fold, at the same time that the biopsy rate increased 2.5 times. The incidence of melanoma may be increasing because more physicians are biopsying more lesions.
In 2007, approximately 8110 people died in the United States from metastatic melanoma.
Melanoma is the third most common skin cancer and the skin cancer responsible for the most skin-cancer-related deaths.
The history of a first-degree relative diagnosed with melanoma and the presence or history of dysplastic nevi significantly increase the risk of a second primary melanoma.
See Risk Factor section below.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Large numbers of benign nevi and atypical nevi
Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) found the evidence insufficient to recommend for or against screening for skin cancer using visual skin exam among asymptomatic adolescents and adults. B
A Cochrane review found no evidence from RCTs to support screening the general adult population as a way of reducing morbidity and mortality from cutaneous melanoma (CM). B

A cost-effectiveness analysis concluded that screening for melanoma in white men every 2 years starting at age 50 or 60 years may be cost-effective, but suggested better studies establishing the accuracy of skin cancer screening exams. B

The USPSTF recommends providing behavioral counseling to adolescents, young adults, children, and parents of young children to minimize UV exposure of fair skinned individuals age 6 months to 24 years and to increase sun protective behavior. Counseling via booklet, video, or computer is effective at reducing sun exposure, especially when focused on effects on appearance rather than health. However, behavioral interventions have not been shown to decrease frequency of sunburns in children or adults, nor definitively improve skin cancer morbidity and mortality. B
A Cochrane review did not find a significant benefit to statins or fibrates for the prevention of CM. B
Examine closely any lesion that a patient states is changing in size, shape, symptoms (itching, tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), and shades of color. Look for the ABCDE criteria (). B
Dermoscopy is more sensitive than the unaided eye in diagnosing cutaneous melanoma (CM), but it requires appropriate training. B
To diagnosie primary CM, perform a narrow-margin excisional biopsy using 1 to 3 mm peripheral and deep margins, whenever possible. B

Partial, incisional, or incomplete diagnostic biopsy may be necessary for lesions that are large or located in anatomically challenging areas (eg, face or acral surfaces). While partial biopsies may lead to incorrect staging and adversely affect treatment plans, they do not lead to worse outcomes (eg, metastasis, recurrence, or survival). B

For biopsy-proven primary CM more than 1 mm thick, sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) performed right before wide excision accurately establishes disease stage but has less certain impact on survival. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Also called atypical moles and can resemble melanoma in situ
Pigmented macules and patches on the face from sun exposure
Stuck-on plaques that may be verrucous with surface cracks
Firm scarlike nodules especially on extremities; may have a brown halo
Tumors that have pigmentation along with pearly raised borders
Nevi that usually do not have the ABCDE criteria
Nevi present at birth or shortly thereafter that can have irregular features; larger ones have greater malignant potential

list.listitem: Dermoscopic criteria can be found at: http://www.dermoscopy.org/.
Clinical staging is based on tumor characteristics, nodal involvement, and the presence of metastasis.

The microstage of cutaneous melanoma is determined on histologic examination by the vertical thickness of the lesion in millimeters (Breslow classification) and/or the anatomic level of local invasion (Clark classification). The Breslow thickness is more reproducible.
See for the Clark classification.
See for clinical staging.

Examine closely any lesion that a patient states is changing in size, shape, symptoms (itching, tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), and shades of color. Patient report of a mole that is changing, especially when supplemented by a previous photo, has good positive predictive value.
The ABCDE criteria are a useful guide to the examination (). Clinical examination is very specific for diagnosis of lymph node metastases.

Keep in mind the "ugly duckling" sign in which a mole or skin growth that looks different from those around it may be a skin cancer. In a prospective study using unaided and dermoscopic images, the ugly duckling sign was more sensitive when defined as all lesions perceived as different, and more specific when defined as only lesions perceived as completely different.

Use good light and magnification to examine suspicious lesions, or a dermatoscope if you have one. Dermoscopy, also called dermatoscopy or epifluorescence microscopy, is more sensitive than the unaided eye in diagnosing cutaneous melanoma (CM).

A Cochrane review concluded that visual inspection, used alone, will lead to missed diagnoses of CM. The systematic review noted inconsistent evidence to support the accuracy of visual inspection in various settings and poor reporting in many of the studies. Additionally, use of algorithms does not appear to improve the accuracy of visual inspection in diagnosing CM.

A 2002 meta-analysis of dermoscopy identified 27 studies of dermoscopy. The authors found that dermoscopy was more accurate than unaided clinical diagnosis for experts but not for nonexperts. A 2008 meta-analysis limited the analysis to high-quality studies comparing dermoscopy with the unaided clinical examination. In 9 studies, the sensitivity was higher for dermoscopy than for clinical examination (87% vs 69%), but specificity was similar (91% vs 88%). Dermoscopy does improve the sensitivity of diagnosis, but it requires adequate training to realize this benefit.

A Cochrane review concluded that the use of dermoscopy as an aid to visual inspection to identify melanoma and atypical intraepidermal melanocytic variants among adults with suspicious lesions referred to clinicians experienced in dermoscopy likely improves the accuracy of diagnosis. Limited evidence supports the use of dermoscopy in primary care, but it may help triage the urgent referral of patients with suspcious lesions, especially among well-trained primary care physicians. Using dermoscopy algorithms may be helpful in dermoscopy training and for less experienced observers, but it is unclear which dermoscopy approach is best for in person dermoscopy.

Another Cochrane review concluded that for diagnostically challenging lesions evaluated by visual inspection and dermoscopy, the use of reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) appears to have better sensitivity and specificity than dermoscopy in diagnosing CM in adults. These findings need prospective confirmation in more realistic settings and among a representative population. A randomized trial enrolling 3165 patients from 3 Italian dermatology referral centers concluded that adjunctive use of RCM for supicious lesions decreases unnecessary excisions and more accurately guides removal of aggressive melanomas.

In patients with risk factors such as family history or many nevi, melanoma tends to present earlier. Those with a family history were more likely to have melanoma on their arms and legs, while those with many nevi were more likely to have melanoma on the trunk.

One or more nevi on an extremity significantly increased risk of CM (and basal cell carcinoma) in a dose-dependent manner with greatest risk in those with at least 15 nevi on an extremity (n = 208,700).

A complete excisional biopsy using narrow (1 to 3 mm) peripheral and deep margins is the gold standard for diagnosing primary cutaneous melanoma (CM). It is the preferred approach if the lesion is small, and can be accomplished using an elliptical (fusiform) approach, punch excision, or deep shave (saucerization) technique.

If the lesion is large or is located in an anatomically challenging area (eg, face, acral surface), performing a partial diagnostic biopsy may be appropriate (eg, saucerization, fusiform incisional technique, or a 4- to 5-mm punch biopsy of the darkest and thickest portion.
While partial, incisional, or incomplete biopsies may lead to incorrect staging and adversely affect treatment plans, they do not lead to worse outcomes (eg, metastasis, recurrence, or survival).

If the pathology from a partial excision is benign and goes against your clinical impression, consider performing a complete re-excision or refer the patient for additional surgery. Avoid doing a superficial shave biopsy if you suspect melanoma because important depth information can be lost. However, a broad scoop shave can often provide better tissue for the pathologist than a single punch biopsy.

For suspected lentigo maligna (LM), the risk of misdiagnosis is high if only punch biopsy specimens are taken. A broad scoop shave biopsy of suspected LM is often recommended because a complete full-thickness fusiform excision of a large lesion on the face can be unnecessarily disfiguring if the ultimate diagnosis is a benign solar lentigo.
For biopsy-proven primary CM more than 1mm thick, sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) performed right before wide excision accurately establishes disease stage but has less certain impact on survival.

Consider initiating a metastatic workup with imaging if the sentinel lymph node is positive for tumor. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the accuracy of different imaging modalities for staging or re-staging melanoma. Ultrasound with fine needle aspiration cytology prior to SNLB may improve diagnosis of nodal metastasis. Most studies have evaluated whole body imaging with PET-CT, but comparative data for MRI or CT is not available. The reviewers suggest the need for studies not only addressing diagnostic accuracy but also evaluating the effects of imaging modalities on overall treatment.

The 2019 American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) clinical practice guidelines (CPG) for the management of primary CM does not recommend baseline labs and imaging studies in the absence of signs or symptoms of metastasis.

Healing of 4-mm punch biopsies by secondary intention was just as good as suturing when occlusive dressings (Tegaderm) were applied at time of punch and changed at 3 days and then weekly thereafter. Gel foam was also used for hemostasis in this study. The cost of gel foam and Tegaderm could be more than the suture, and this method required a 3-day follow-up visit to remove the gel foam and change the occlusive dressing.
A Cochrane review did not find a clear role for exfoliative cytology using Tzanck smear of skin scrapings as a non-invasive diagnostic option for CM.

Similarly, two separate Cochrane reviews found insufficient evidence for high-frequency ultrasound (20 MHz or higher) and optical coherence tomography (a microscopic imaging modality using near-infrared light) to diagnose CM.

A Cochrane review evaluating the role of artificial intelligence (AI) or computer-assisted diagnosis (CAD) techniques for dermoscopy or spectroscopy found CAD techniques to be highly sensitive in diagnosing CM among patients referred to skin specialists. Data is unclear whether CAD systems result to actual changes in clinical management or whether they are useful in the primary care setting.

A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for AI-based smartphone applications to diagnose CM. They concluded that these apps currently have poor diagnostic accuracy. One prospective RCT in Sweden involving 36 primary care clinics evaluating 253 lesions suspicious for melanoma in 228 patients found the Dermalyser app (from AI Medical Technology) to have a high negative predictive value for melanoma identification by primary care physicians. The app appears to accurately identify lesions that can be monitored without a biopsy as long as the app and physician both agree that the lesion is low risk. Additionally, it may help prioritize lesions that need to be referred when both app and physician have a high suspicion for melanoma. Before AI-based smartphone apps become widely adopted, more rigorous trials evaluating the impact on referral and biopsy rates are needed, as well as patient-oriented outcomes like morbidity, mortality, and health-related quality of life. This particular app was also not evaluated on dark-skinned persons since it used Swedish patients.

While teledermatology has become increasingly available, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for its accuracy in diagnosing CM and its utility in triaging patients from primary to specialty care. More prospective and pragmatic trials are necessary.
Two clinical decision rules have been developed and validated to predict survival following treatment for primary melanoma.
Examine closely any lesion that a patient states is changing in size, shape, symptoms (itching, tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), and shades of color, looking for ABCDE criteria.
Keep in mind that there are at least 5 different categories of melanomas, and these have different features ().
Dermoscopy is more sensitive than the unaided eye in diagnosing melanoma.
Biopsy any suspicious lesion.

Treatment of biopsy-proven invasive cutaneous melanoma (CM) requires wide excision using the following surgical margins: 1 cm for lesions 1.0 mm or less in tumor thickness (Breslow); 1 to 2 cm for lesions 1.1 to 2.0 mm thick; and 2 cm for lesions more than 2.0 mm thick. A
For biopsy-proven MIS, wide excision using 0.5 to 1 cm surgical margins or MMS is recommended. For lentigo maligna, MMS is preferred. B
Completion lymph node dissection (CLND) following a positive SLNB may improve disease staging and regional disease control but does not appear to improve melanoma-specific and overall survival. B
Adjuvant treatment of stage II to III CM using interferon-alpha improves disease-free survival and overall survival (NNT = 35 to prevent 1 death over 5 years). A

For stage IV CM, newer systemic treatments like biochemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, anti-CTLA4 and anti-PD1 monoclonal antibodies), small-molecule targeted drugs (eg, BRAF and MEK inhibitors), and anti-angiogenic drugs appear more effective than conventional chemotherapy. A

The 2019 AAD CPG recommends the use of topical imiquimod 5% cream as second-line treatment for MIS, LM type, if surgery is not possible as the primary treatment or as adjuvant therapy after surgical excision. Shared decision-making is paramount, especially if imiquimod is chosen as the primary treatment instead of surgical excision, and discussion should cover risks, benefits, and uncertainties of nonsurgical treatment.
There is no evidence from RCTs of a survival benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy in addition to surgery in the treatment of stage I CM.
A Cochrane review evaluating interferon-alpha for adjuvant treatment of stage II to III CM found that it improves both disease-free and overall survival.

In an RCT of 951 patients with stage III CM, ipilimumab 10 mg/kg every 3 weeks for 4 doses and then every 3 months for up to 3 years led to an increase in 5 year recurrence free survival rates (40.8% vs 30.3%, p <0.001, NNT = 10) and an increase in overall 5 year survival (65.4% vs 54.4%, p = 0.001, NNT = 9). Adverse events are relatively common and ipilimumab causes death in about 1% of patients.

In patients with stage III CM and the V600K or BRAF V600E mutations, the combination of dabrafenib and trametinib improved 3 year relapse free survival compared with placebo (58% vs 39%, p <0.001, NNT = 5). Fever, fatigue, nausea, and headache each occurred in at least 39% of patients and 26% of patients had the drug discontinued due to adverse effects. An extended follow-up of this study (median 8.3 years) found higher overall survival with the combination therapy although it was not quite statistically significant (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.62 - 1.01). A signifiant benefit was seen for patients with the BRAF V600E mutation, and also a greater likelihood of relapse free and metastasis free survival.

A trial randomized 423 patients with resectable stage III melanoma to: Group 1) 2 rounds of neoadjuvant ipilimumab plus nivolumab followed by surgery or to Group 2) surgery followed by 12 cycles of adjuvant nivolumab. The 12 month event-free survival was higher with Group 1 (83.7% vs 57.2%, p < .001, NNT = 4). Twelve month recurrence free survival in the neoadjuvant group was 95% if they had a major response, 76% with a partial response and 57% if no response.

A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of neoadjuvant treatment (ie, induction treatment to shrink primary tumor prior to surgical excision) for stage III and IV CM. Moreover, it may lead to more adverse events.

In a trial of adults with unresectable stage III or IV CM, an industry sponsored trial found improved survival and decreased rates of disease progression for patients randomized to pembrolizumab (anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody) versus ipilimumab (anti-CTLA4 monoclonal antibody), with similar adverse event profiles.

Patients (n=313) with resectable stage IIIB to IVC melanoma were randomized to neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, surgery, and adjuvant pembrolizumab (neoadjuvant–adjuvant group) or to surgery followed by pembrolizumab (200 mg intravenously for about 1 year (adjuvant group). At 2 years, event-free survival was significantly more likely in the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group (72% vs 49%).

In a study of patients with stage III or IV CM, 3 year survival was significantly greater with the combination of nivolumab (anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody) and ipilimumab (58%) than with nivolumab alone (52%) or ipilimumab (34%).

A randomized trial in 906 patients with Stage IIIB, IIIC, or IV CM compared nivolumab with ipilimumab. Patients randomized to nivolumab had a greater likelihood of 12 month recurrence free survival (70.5% vs 60.8%, p <0.001, NNT = 10) and were significantly less likely to discontinue treatment due to adverse events (9.7% vs 42.6%, NNH = 3).

In 870 patients with stage III melanoma and the BRAF V600E or V600K mutations, a randomized trial found that the likelihood of 5 year survival without relapse was significantly higher with dabrafenib + trametinib than with placebo (52% vs 36%, NNT = 6).

An RCT compared combined nivolumab + ipilimumab with nivolomab or ipilimumab alone in 945 patients with Stage III or IV melanoma. The medium overall survival was 60 months in the combination therapy group, 37 months in the nivolomab only group, and only 20 months in the ipilimumab only group. 5 year overall survival was 52% with combination therapy, 44% with nivolumab, and 26% with ipilimumab (NNT for comparisons 12 and 4, respectively). A 10 year follow-up of the same study found that median overall survival was still higher with combination therapy (71.9 months versus 20 to 37 months with each drug alone).

A trial randomized 168 patients with unresectable stage IIIC or IV melanoma to receive autologously derived tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) or ipilimumab at 3 mg/kilogram. Overall survival (25.8 vs 18.9 months) and progression free survival (7.2 months vs 3.1 months) were both significantly higher with TIL.

A Cochrane review evaluating systemic treatments for stage IV CM concluded that high-quality evidence supports the superiority of newer therapies like small-molecule targeted drugs over traditional chemotherapy. Biochemotherapy (chemotherapy plus interferon-alpha and interleukin-2) and BRAF inhibitors appear better than chemotherapy in improving progression-free survival. BRAF inhibitors and anti-PD1 monoclonal antibodies, compared to chemotherapy, improve overall survival. However, monochemotherapy and polychemotherapy have similar progression-free and overall survival. Additionally, biochemotherapy does not improve overall survival and is associated with more toxicity than chemotherapy.

Combination therapies seem better than monotherapy for stage IV CM. Anti-PD1 monoclonal antibodies, alone or combined with anti-CTLA4, have better progression-free survival than anti-CTLA4 monotherapy. BRAF inhibitors combined with MEK inhibitors have better overall survival than BRAF inhibitor monotherapy.

For stage IV CM patients with BRAF mutation, combination therapy with BRAF and MEK inhibitors is the most effective treatment, resulting in improved progression-free survival. In contrast, the most acceptable and least toxic therapy are anti-PD1 monoclonal antibodies.

In a series of 94 patients with CM metastatic to brain, all were given nivolumab + ipilimumab every 3 weeks for 4 doses, followed by nivollumab ever 2 weeks. The rate of stable disease for 6 months was 2%, of partial response was 30%, and of complete response was 26%. Adverse events, however, were relatively common.

A combined analysis of two RCTs compared the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib + the MEK inhibitor trametinib to treatment with a single monoclonal antibody in patients with the BRAF mutation. Overall survival was 37% at 4 years and 34% at 5 years, while a complete response occurred in 19% who had overall survival of 71%.

A study identified 714 patients with previously untreated metastatic melanoma who expressed the LAG-3 and PD-L1 mutations. They were randomized to relatlimab + nivolumab or nivolumab alone. Progression free survival was improved with combination therapy (median 10.1 vs 4.6 months) but overall survival is not reported (despite being listed as a secondary outcome).

In patients with metastatic uveal melanoma who were positive for HLAA* 02:01, a randomized trial with 378 patients found that overall survival was significantly higher with tebentafusp than with the investigator's choice of control therapy (73% vs 59%, NNT = 7). After 3 years, survival remained greater in the tebentafusp group (27% vs 18%).
Surgical resection is the treatment of choice for stage I and II CM.

For biopsy-proven melanoma in-situ, wide excision using 0.5 to 1 cm surgical margins or Mohs Microscopic Surgery (MMS) is generally recommended. For lentigo maligna, MMS is preferred. A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating the surgical management of MIS and LM.

Treatment of biopsy-proven invasive CM requires wide excision using the following surgical margins: 1 cm for lesions 1.0 mm or less in tumor thickness (Breslow); 1 to 2 cm for lesions 1.1 to 2.0 mm thick; and 2 cm for lesions more than 2.0 mm thick.
For stage I CM, evidence from an observational study suggests that MMS and wide excision have comparable survival outcomes.

An retrospective cohort study compared outcomes in 1179 patients who had a 5 mm margin with those receiving a 10 mm margin for a T1a cutaneous melanoma. Melanoma specific mortality was non-significantly higher in the narrow margin group (4.2% vs 1.8%). Factors associated with higher mortality included Breslow thickness > 0.4 mm and mitotic rate > 1/mm2.

Wide excision (2 cm or more) of CM less than 2 mm thick is unlikely to improve survival or reduce recurrent disease based on a meta-analysis of RCTs. A Cochrane review of 5 trials with over 3200 participants came to the same conclusion.

An open label multicentre RCT studied 936 clinically staged CM in ages 75 or younger diagnosed with melanoma thicker than 2 mm on trunk or limbs. Random allocation to treatment either to 2 cm or 4 cm excision margin showed 2 cm excision was safe at median follow up of 19.6 years.

Based on evidence from 2 RCTs and retrospective studies, completion lymph node dissection (CLND) following a positive SLNB may improve disease staging and regional disease control but does not appear to improve melanoma-specific and overall survival. Current guidelines recommend offering patients with positive SLNB either CLND or active nodal basin surveillance with ultrasound.
Mistletoe (Viscum album) extracts and hormone therapies are not beneficial.
A trial randomized 436 patients with resected stage IA to III melanoma to vitamin D 100,000 IU monthly or placebo. There was no benefit to vitamin D supplementation.
Psychosocial guidance and rehabilitation, if needed, constitute an important task of the caring physician.
Patients with advanced melanoma require a coordinated multiprofessional approach with input from a specialist palliative care team.
Indoor tanning slightly increases melanoma risk.
Radiation therapy is used in certain circumstances for primary and metastatic melanoma.
It is estimated that the lifetime risk that a mole will become melanoma in a 50-year-old man is 1 in 2000; in a 50-year-old woman, it is 1 in 9000. B
Patients with 1 melanoma have an 11.4% risk at 5 years of developing a second melanoma, with around half (5.5%) of the cases recurring in the first year. B

Suggested surveillance interval for stage IA to IIA cutaneous melanoma (CM) is every 6 to 12 months for 2 to 5 years, then annually thereafter. For stage IIB or more advanced CM, follow-up interval is every 3 to 6 months for the first 2 years, every 6 months for 3 to 5 years, then annually thereafter. C

In 1 meta-analysis, 0.7% of congenital melanocytic nevi (CMN) reported in the medical literature underwent malignant transformation. However, 75% arose in large bathing trunk nevi greater than 40 cm in diameter. Because of the higher rate in small studies, suggesting selection bias, this figure of 0.7% probably represents an upper bound. The largest population-based study found that 0.2% of all newborns were registered as having CMN, of whom only 0.05% underwent malignant transformation after a median follow-up of 10 years.

Using a theoretical model and existing sources of data, it is estimated that the lifetime risk that a mole will become melanoma in a 50-year-old man is 1 in 2000; in a 50-year-old woman, it is 1 in 9000.
In 1 study, 230 medium-sized CMN (1.5-19.9 cm) in 227 patients were prospectively followed from 1955 to 1996, and not a single melanoma occurred in the congenital nevi.

Patients with 1 melanoma have an 11.4% risk at 5 years of developing a second melanoma, with about half (5.5%) of the cases recurring in the first year. Both family history of a first-degree relative with melanoma and personal history of dysplastic nevi significantly increase the risk. All of these patients merit close follow-up screening for melanoma.

See for melanoma survival by stage and tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) classification. Survival is shown for an older US study and a newer Danish registry study. The Danish study found that mortality curves largely flattened out by 6 to 8 years. The 10 year melanoma specific mortality for stage IA was only 1.4%.
A 31 gene expression profile can identify patients with stage I - III melanoma at increased risk for recurrence or metastasis.

Suggested surveillance interval for stage IA to IIA CM is every 6 to 12 months for 2 to 5 years, then annually thereafter. For stage IIB or more advanced CM, follow-up interval is every 3 to 6 months for the first 2 years, every 6 months for 3 to 5 years, then annually thereafter.

Imaging techniques including ultrasound of lymph nodes, CT, or whole-body PET-CT may be considered in the follow-up of high-risk patients, that is, those with thick primary tumors or following treatment of metastases.
Sun protection and avoidance is paramount.
Regular self-examination of the skin is recommended, although clinical trials to support its efficacy are lacking.
Similarly, regular physical examinations by persons trained in melanoma detection are often recommended for high-risk patients, but evidence is lacking.

The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends providing behavioral counseling to adolescents, young adults, children, and parents of young children to minimize UV exposure of fair skinned individuals age 6 months to 24 years and to increase sun protective behavior. Counseling via booklet, video, or computer is effective at reducing sun exposure, especially when focused on effects on appearance rather than health. However, behavioral interventions have not been shown to decrease frequency of sunburns in children or adults, nor definitively improve skin cancer morbidity and mortality.

feature.caption: The ABCDE Mnemonic for Melanoma Diagnosis.

tr.td: Asymmetry
Melanomas are usually asymmetric: a line through the middle will not create matching halves. Benign nevi are usually round and symmetric.
Border
The borders of melanomas are often uneven and may have scalloped or notched edges. Benign nevi have smoother, more even borders.
Color
Variation in color. Benign nevi are usually a single shade of brown. Melanomas are often varied shades of brown, tan, or black. As melanomas progress, they may appear red, white, and blue.
Diameter
Diameter of 6 mm or greater. Melanomas tend to grow larger than most nevi.
Evolving
Evolving could be in changes in size, shape, symptoms (itching, tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), and shades of color.
Superficial spreading melanoma
Asymmetric with irregular borders and multiple colors
Can occur anywhere, commonly on the upper back, legs in women and trunk in men
All ages but accounts for most melanomas in young persons
Nodular melanoma
Most often black, raised, and thickened; may have other colors
Anywhere
No specific demographics
LM
Similar to superficial spreading type in appearance
Face, ears
Average age of onset is 65 years old
Acral lentiginous melanoma
2-8 in white persons: higher percentage in dark-skinned persons
May start as a dark macule on the palms or soles or under a nail
On the hands and feet by definition, especially the palms, soles, and subungual areas
Accounts for a larger percentage of melanomas in dark-skinned individuals
Amelanotic melanoma
Less than 1%
Lacks pigment and may be nodular
Anywhere
No specific demographics

feature.caption: Clark Classification of Level of Invasion.

tr.td: Ia
Lesions involving only the epidermis (in situ melanoma); not an invasive lesion. Tumor is less than 1 mm without ulceration and Clark's level II/III.
Ib
Lesions involving only the epidermis (in situ melanoma); not an invasive lesion. Tumor is less than 1 mm with ulceration or Clark's level IV/V.
II
Invasion of the papillary dermis but does not reach the papillary-reticular dermal interface.
III
Invasion fills and expands the papillary dermis but does not penetrate the reticular dermis.
IV
Invasion into the reticular dermis but not into the subcutaneous tissue.
V
Invasion through the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue.
